title: Black holes: an end, an edge and four clues (a CI fixture)
dek: How one forms, what its edge is and how we know, in short steps (a CI fixture).

states.alt: The end of a star many times the Sun’s mass. Only a star above about eight times the Sun’s mass ends this way. In the middle of its life hydrogen fuses in its core, and the pressure from that energy balances gravity.

The end of a star many times the Sun’s mass. Only a star above about eight times the Sun’s mass ends this way. Its core fuel used up, the pressure that held the core up falls away and gravity wins: the core collapses inward. The picture draws the eye to the core.

The end of a star many times the Sun’s mass. Only a star above about eight times the Sun’s mass ends this way. The collapse throws off the star’s outer layers in a supernova explosion, and what is left of the core can be a black hole. The picture draws the eye to what is left.

Two black holes drawn to the same scale, one four times as massive as the other. The edge of a black hole is its event horizon, about three kilometres from the centre for each Sun’s mass of the hole, so four times the mass means a horizon four times as wide. Light aimed straight outward from outside the horizon can get away; inside it even light aimed outward falls farther in. The horizon is a boundary in space, not a surface. The smaller hole is marked. The picture draws the eye to the horizon.

Two black holes drawn to the same scale, one four times as massive as the other. The edge of a black hole is its event horizon, about three kilometres from the centre for each Sun’s mass of the hole, so four times the mass means a horizon four times as wide. Light aimed straight outward from outside the horizon can get away; inside it even light aimed outward falls farther in. The horizon is a boundary in space, not a surface. The larger hole is marked. The picture draws the eye to the horizon.

A star and a black hole of the same mass, with the same pull on a faraway object. Far from either, gravity depends only on the mass and the distance, so a black hole does not pull harder than a star of its mass, and it does not suck in everything around it. Near the horizon it is very different. Not to scale: the black hole is far smaller than the star. The picture draws the eye to the black hole.

Three stars circling a point where nothing shines, on orbits drawn as circles for simplicity. The nearer a star is to the centre, the faster it moves, and all three orbits follow from one large mass hidden there. This is one clue to a black hole, but it does not prove one by itself. The picture draws the eye to the centre of the orbits.

Gas spiralling towards a black hole forms a disc that heats as it falls: the nearer the hole, the hotter the gas, and the hottest inner gas glows in X-rays. The glow is drawn in false colour, since X-rays cannot be seen, and the black hole itself gives out no light. This is one clue to a black hole, but it does not prove one by itself. The picture draws the eye to the disc.

Two black holes spiral close together, orbiting faster and faster. The ripples in space they make grow stronger and quicker, a rising chirp on the graph of wave strength over time. This is one clue to a black hole, but it does not prove one by itself. The picture draws the eye to the graph of wave strength.

A bright ring of glowing gas round a dark patch, as in images made with a network of radio telescopes. The dark patch is the black hole’s shadow: light from behind it that passes this close is bent into the hole. The shadow is about two and a half times as wide as the horizon, which lies inside it, so it is not the horizon itself. This is one clue to a black hole, but it does not prove one by itself. The picture draws the eye to the shadow.

blocks.text: Only a star many times the Sun’s mass can end as a black hole. In the middle of its life, fusion in the core pushes outward as hard as gravity pulls inward.

stops.simple: A massive star holds itself up with fusion.

blocks.text: When its core fuel is used up, the pressure that held the core up falls away. Gravity wins, and the core collapses.

stops.prompt: Which star can end as a black hole?
options: A star many times the Sun’s mass
stops.explain: Only a star with far more mass than the Sun has a core that collapses this way. A star like the Sun leaves a white dwarf.
stops.twist: The Sun is the star we know best, which makes it the easy guess. It is too light.

blocks.text: The collapse throws off the star’s outer layers in a supernova, and what is left of the core can be a black hole.

stops.simple: A supernova can leave a black hole.

blocks.text: The edge of a black hole is its event horizon. It is a boundary in space, not a surface. Inside it nothing can return, not even light.

stops.simple: The horizon is a boundary, not a surface.

blocks.text: A black hole four times as massive has a horizon four times as wide.

stops.simple: Four times the mass, four times the horizon.

blocks.text: Far away a black hole pulls just as a star of its mass would. It does not suck in everything around it.

stops.simple: Far away the pull is the same.

stops.prompt: If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of the same mass, how would Earth’s orbit change?
stops.explain: Gravity far away depends on the mass and the distance only, and both are the same.
stops.twist: Black holes have a name for swallowing things, which makes spiralling in feel likely. That is only true very close.

blocks.text: Stars that circle a point where nothing shines show that a large mass is hidden there. That is one clue.
Gas spiralling in heats up, and the hottest gas glows in X-rays. The colours here are false, because X-rays cannot be seen.
Two black holes that spiral together send out ripples in space. They grow stronger and quicker until the merger.
Images of glowing gas show a dark patch, the black hole’s shadow. It is wider than the horizon, so it is not the horizon itself.

stops.simple: The shadow is not the horizon.

stops.prompt: Black hole A has twice the mass of black hole B. How do their horizons compare?
options: A’s is four times as wide
stops.explain: The horizon’s radius goes as the mass, so twice the mass means twice the radius.
stops.twist: Four is tempting, because areas go as squares. The radius goes straight with the mass.
stops.simple: Twice the mass, twice the horizon.

asides.title: Where this stops
asides.text: The picture draws nothing at the centre, because the centre is not understood. The black holes here are illustrative, and no one clue proves a black hole by itself.

captions: Only a massive star’s collapse can leave one.
The horizon is a boundary that goes with the mass.
Together, several clues make the case.

askSuggestions: What would change if the numbers were different?
Where does this picture stop being true?
